Media Digest: A Fulfilling Literary Life
Charlie Markbreiter's profile of author Isabel Pabán Freed  ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌

Media Digest: A Fulfilling Literary Life
Charlie Markbreiter's profile of author Isabel Pabán Freed
Journalism and AI:
Addressing Fears, Anxieties, and Concerns
Wednesday, October 28, 2026
10:00 AM PT / 1:00 PM ET
Free to attend
In this webinar panel, three seasoned journalists —
Taylor Lorenz
,
Alexandra Marvar
, and
Brian Merchant
— will share how media workers can navigate AI tools and the various ways in which this technology has transformed the industry.
This panel will touch upon how legacy media outlets are coming up with AI rules, and what writers can do to protect their work. In addition, the panelists will discuss larger questions about how AI has changed the industry: Is it possible to integrate these tools in a workflow without plagiarizing other writers' work? Is there a double standard of media outlets banning freelancers from using these tools, while editors use in-house AI tools? What does it mean to have original prose in a time when LLMs can mimic style?
Register
here
.
Okay, Diva: The Fulfilling Literary Life of Isabel Pabán Freed
By Charlie Markbreiter
Share on
Bluesky

Notes
Isabel Pabán Freed doesn’t have an agent. She has never published with a major or small publisher. But physical copies of her books are stocked and sold at independent bookstores internationally. A paperback copy of her first novel,
School
(2023), “made its way through an entire Australian trans lesbian polycule,” Pabán Freed told me. How did this happen? The most important, most obvious answer is that Pabán Freed’s books are good; the Marx Bro answer, the one that zips straight to the means of production, is that Pabán Freed’s books are self-published.
Long-maligned as a “
vanity project
,” self-publishing has been
on the rise
since at least
2024
. Authors can publish their creations on platforms like Inkitt, which uses AI to
ghostwrite
sequels for Galatea, its premium subscription app. Galatea’s novels frequently hit a million dollars in sales, and the company has raised a hundred million in VC funding. But while Galatea invests in popular genres like romance and fantasy, literary fiction, roughly
two percent
of the market, has not received the same attention.
Meanwhile, according to
reporting
from
404 Media
, AI developer
Amazon
has trained its Large Language Models (LLMs) on “rare” books, which it bulk-buys and then destroys. “Rare” includes anything that is hard to find online and was produced outside the commercial literary market — including self-published texts. While book publishers and distributors often see these rare books as worthless, they’re valuable to AI developers, who want to train their LLMs on language produced pre-LLMs.
For Pabán Freed, however, the value of self-publishing is that it’s a way around commercial taste. Instead of haplessly ping-ponging between Big 5 presses and Substack, Pabán Freed, to quote a (self-published) essay, gets to be “a total cunt. I’m a diva! I do the things I want to do with my writing because why else bother?” Her
essay
is titled “The Fall of Isabel Pabán Freed.”
+
Pabán Freed is thirty. She grew up in Texas. Her parents are academics in math and physics, and her mother is from Spain. She began reading literature after picking up
Inherent Vice
by Thomas Pynchon at age thirteen. As part of her high school
quizbowl
team training, she began systematically reading and memorizing the classics.
School
opens with an undergraduate self-immolating on the main quad; in the cafeteria, undergraduates discuss a video clip of the suicide, which has since been erased. The university resembles Stanford, which Pabán Freed attended. Her second novel,
It’s the Characters!
(2025), is a stoner neo-noir set in San Francisco; her third book, an essay collection,
In the Forum of Madness
(2025), includes pieces such as “
What a trans woman who never tucked thinks about taping a dick that’s struggling to stand up again
,” “
I Was Sexually Assaulted on a Train in 2019
,” and “
basically every tweet i ever wrote except for all the ones i deleted because i got obsessed with the idea that They Were Going to Kill Me, or, on being _unwell
.”
Stylistically, Pabán Freed has been
compared
to David Foster Wallace. Writer Katherine Packert Burke said that
School
was “the main thing I’ve read, since
Infinite Jest
, which reminds me of
Infinite Jest.
” It makes sense: they both enjoy adverbs; they both publish fiction and criticism; they both combine talk-y, velvety interior monologues, across a cascading array of characters, with the
detail-oriented
worldbuilding available to writers who could have pursued careers in STEM (Pabán Freed minored in comp science; Foster Wallace pursued modal logic and mathematics as part of his English and philosophy double major). Pabán Freed is the one who tells me about the Foster Wallace
egg
rumors: an ex, writer Gale Walden,
saying
Foster Wallace “was always aggrieved that men couldn’t wear skirts”; that he “wore other clothes of mine.” In
Consider the Lobster
, his 2005 essay collection, Foster Wallace expresses the same man/skirt sentiment in a piece called “Authority and American Usage.”
Both Foster Wallace and Pabán Freed are also both very funny. In
School
, for instance, all the characters have last names based off of foods: Billy Bean-Couscous, a protagonist named Johnny Soufflé.
School
is dedicated to “the petty bourgeois.” While Foster Wallace’s humor can be sadistic, almost bullying (think, for instance of
Infinite Jest
’s “Poor Tony,” who is repeatedly placed in humiliating, dysphoric circumstances), novelist
Sebastian Castillo
described Pabán Freed as “
incredibly funny… but also quite thoughtful in her humor, a humor with real feeling and intelligence behind it, which to me is the most important kind.”
When I ask about Foster Wallace’s influence, Pabán Freed said that the writer who most influenced her work is actually Virginia Woolf. As Woolf once wrote in a 1940 letter, “It’s odd, for I’m not regularly musical, but I always think of my books as music before I write them.” Pabán Freed, who compares Woolf’s books to musical scores, worked out
School
’s sentence structures by listening to rappers like MF DOOM and Pusha T, as well as musicians like Kate Bush, SOPHIE, and Pink Floyd.
But the comparison makes sense on the level of character as well: the way Woolf used free indirect discourse to transit from panoramic, slow motion social situations to the inside of a character’s heart, first one and then the other, through what she described as a “tunneling process,” a way of “digging out caves” behind her characters.
The other thing that Pabán Freed and Woolf have in common of course is that they both self-published. Woolf was in fact almost entirely self-published, releasing her books through Hogarth Press, which she ran with her husband, Leonard Woolf. Hogarth began in 1917, when the Woolfs purchased a hand-operated printer press and began using it in their dining room.
Jacob’s Room
, Virginia’s first novel with Hogarth, was published in 1922;
Mrs. Dalloway
(1925) and
To the Lighthouse
(1927), arguably her two most famous novels, were both self-published.
Pabán Freed began releasing her books on a website called
Bartleby.Life
, named for the Melville character. Each book (which Pabán Freed formats, with lightly magnified serif font) is available via PDF or eBook. Readers who want a physical version can buy one from
IngramSpark
, which prints individual copies of self-published books on demand, complete with ISBN numbers and bar codes. The three books have grossed $3,200 total; $1,200 of the profits from
School
have been donated to incarcerated people.
When I asked Pabán Freed how she began self-publishing, she said she “wrote
School
with the plan to self-pub, lost my job because bipolar in 2023, thought it’d be good to get paid so tried getting an agent, didn’t work, went with the original plan. Second book, I also tried to get an agent just to see, didn’t work, went with the original plan. Third book, didn’t bother.”
Part of why this works is that writing isn’t Pabán Freed’s main source of income. Instead, she has done “stable, relatively undemanding office jobs for seven years so that I would never have to depend on my writing to pay my bills.” She currently lives in San Francisco and works at a bookstore. Before that, she was an editor at a technical press and did customer service for a typesetting company.
When we describe self-publishing as a “vanity project,” where is the vanity from? In Hollywood, “vanity projects” imply a triumph of personal wealth and power over good taste and market demand (think, for instance, of J. Lo’s musical film
This is Me…Now
, which she self-funded for $20 million). In Woolf's case, the term’s implicit class critique is salient. Virginia came from a well-off English family; Leonard grew up in a Jewish family under “
economic difficulty
,” but managed to assimilate into British society, attending Cambridge on scholarship. This inherited wealth and social status allowed the Woolfs to purchase a printing press and fund Hogarth, which began as a hobby but became profitable enough to
serve
as Leonard’s sole source of income.
But independence from market demands also gave Hogarth independence from market taste. In addition to Virginia’s work, Hogarth also published paradigm-shifting texts like T.S. Eliot’s
The Wasteland
to
The Standard Edition of the Complete Psychological Works of Sigmund Freud
. It is hard to imagine twentieth-century culture without either of these books.
Today, self-publishing physical books is more accessible. When I asked Pabán Freed whether her model is replicable, she said, “Very.” She didn’t have seed funding or start-up capital. Her biggest advantage was already having typesetting and computer programming skills. To produce physical books, Pabán Freed does the typesetting digitally herself. The file is then sent to IngramSpark, which creates the physical copies. When Pabán Freed couldn’t do cover art, she commissioned images from
painter
Zhanpei Fang.
Setting aside the cost of typesetting, editing, and creating a cover, it’s possible to self-publish a physical book at no cost, according to Pabán Freed. IngramSpark’s publishing tools are free and the service also offers U.S.-based authors a unique ISBN free of charge.
Maybe that’s vanity — writing what you want when you want it; if so, then more writers should get to be vain. Everyone should be able to write and publish what they want because they want to, because it is pleasurable and useful. Or, in Marx Bro terms, because it has use-value, not just exchange-value. When I asked Katherine Burke if she owns any of Pabán Freed’s books, she said, “I own physical copies of all of them.”
While Pabán Freed is grateful that her work has found readers, that isn’t why she writes; she writes because writing and books are useful and good in and of themselves. As Pabán Freed writes in “The Fall of Isabel Pabán Freed,” in a quote she sent to me, "I write because I love and believe in writing… I write and read to live a better, richer, more profound life.”
Interview with Benjamin Moser
On the latest Study Hall Podcast
episode
, Benjamin Moser, a Pulitzer Prize-winning author, discussed his new book
Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History
. In this conversation, Moser talked about his writing process and why he’s drawn to the figure of the conscious pariah.
The Conscious Pariah ft. Benjamin Moser
Podcast Episode · The Study Hall Podcast · September 28 · 53m

Asteah Herndon on stepping out of the political media bubble.
Katie Notopoulos on tech reporting.
